brief.head: Brains, not stomachs
brief.text: Indians are taught at school that pop­u­la­tion is the country’s big­gest prob­lem. Amit Varma dis­agrees: peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs[[x2]][[x1]], and what gets blamed on num­bers is failed gov­er­nance. {001-C05}

brief.head: Rather be poor where?
brief.text: Would you rather be poor in the USA[[x3]] or Bangladesh? Everyone picks the USA, Amit Varma said, though it is more un­equal. India’s prob­lem is poverty, not in­equal­ity[[x4]]. {001-C06}

brief.head: Old songs, new sales
brief.text: Old music now out­sells new, Amit Varma re­ported. Ajay Shah doubted that tastes fixed in youth ex­plain it: *Dark Side of the Moon* re­mains among the most suc­cess­ful al­bums ever. {001-C14}

brief.head: Oral history
brief.text: *The Seen and the Unseen*, Amit Varma’s other pod­cast, has be­come oral his­tory, Ajay Shah said: deep dives of three to eight hours into one in­ter­est­ing per­son at a time. {001-R22}

brief.head: Uncles only
brief.text: Only men can be un­cles, Amit Varma con­ceded while ex­plain­ing the com­pli­ment he had been paid. Women, he sug­gested, “can be Karens, I guess.” {001-J05}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah begin a weekly conversation
lead.head: Of snakes, seagulls and uncles

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 1

body: The first episode of *Everything is Everything* began with a prom­ise and a hair­cut. Amit Varma said the new weekly show would talk “not just about the pro­found, but also the pro­fane”. Ajay Shah asked at once how he got that in­ter­est­ing hair­cut. {001-J01}
It was the vil­lage barber’s work, done with no elec­tric­ity.
The thread through what fol­lowed was the image that gives the episode its title: peo­ple as works in progress, half­way from coal and half­way to di­a­mond, able to re­write them­selves.
## The cobra and the code

Shah’s sub­ject was an­i­mals. India’s big four ven­omous snakes, he said, are very dif­fer­ent from one an­other. The cobra lives around peo­ple, flashes its hood and often strikes with its mouth closed: it is “much less dan­ger­ous than is widely con­sid­ered”.
Seagulls are the re­verse: grace­ful to look at, they kill pi­geons and gouge chunks from the backs of baby whales.

We pass no moral judg­ment on an­i­mals, Varma ob­served, though hu­mans, also an­i­mals, are judged for ev­ery­thing. Shah’s an­swer was hard­ware and soft­ware. A new­born king cobra is hard-coded for life; hu­mans run an op­er­at­ing sys­tem of cul­ture that they can ex­am­ine and re­write. “So cul­ture, that plas­tic­ity is what makes us human,” he said. {001-C01}

Varma replied that char­ac­ter is con­tin­gent, shaped by genes and cir­cum­stances. But even if there is no free will, he ar­gued, “for civ­i­liza­tion to progress, we must be­have as if there is.” {001-C02}
Shah’s rule for the striv­ing in be­tween was to judge the al­go­rithm, not the out­come: “don’t judge a de­ci­sion by its out­come be­cause the world is prob­a­bilis­tic.” {001-C03}
## Uncles and anti-uncles
Varma’s sub­ject began with a com­pli­ment. The writer Shrayana Bhattacharya once told him he was an “anti-uncle”: open to ideas, ready to change his mind and to en­gage with any­one. {001-S05}

That led Varma to Paul Graham’s essay *The Four Quadrants of Conformism*. The ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded make the loud­est noise on so­cial media with­out say­ing any­thing new, Varma said, and they hold back progress. {001-C04}

Shah, by his own de­scrip­tion a “card car­ry­ing econ­o­mist”, was kinder. “People are not wood, peo­ple are not stones, peo­ple are op­ti­miz­ers,” he said. {001-C07} Many un­cles, in his view, ride an ide­ol­ogy to­wards power and will turn on a dime.

He cited his old teacher Timur Kuran’s idea of pref­er­ence fal­si­fi­ca­tion: be­fore com­mu­nism fell, ev­ery­one in East Germany and the USSR pro­fessed the of­fi­cial be­liefs, and in their hearts no­body held them. {001-C08}
Criticism, Shah added, suf­fers from a mar­ket fail­ure. The critic takes the at­tacks, while the progress be­longs to ev­ery­one.
## A life in every book
Books, Varma ar­gued, let us col­lect far more dots than ex­pe­ri­ence does, and fic­tion lets us live other lives. Shah added that every great book of ideas gives its reader one extra life.

The hosts ended on a puz­zle. Far more peo­ple today can make art or do sci­ence than ever be­fore, so where are the mas­ter­pieces? Funding for sci­ence has risen a mil­lion­fold, Shah said, and yet “some­thing about the ma­chine, some­thing about the mod­ern world, is in­ter­fer­ing with the great leaps.” {001-C15}
All that money, he grum­bled, had pro­duced food de­liv­ery apps and LLMs. Varma’s rem­edy: unin­stall the apps and cook our own food.
Varma, new to video, joked that he has “a face for audio”. {001-J12}

second.label: Luck and art
second.head: Play it again, please
second.deck: Amit Varma on the listener who talked Billy Joel’s song onto the radio

pic.caption: Billy Joel at the Metropolitan Opera premiere in New York in 2009

body: Billy Joel’s *Piano Man* al­most dis­ap­peared into obliv­ion, Amit Varma said, and Joel was not going to make any more music. {001-S09}

Then one man who loved the song went from radio sta­tion to radio sta­tion, ask­ing them to play it. At a big sta­tion he fi­nally struck a deal with some­one, and “al­most bribed him in a sense”, Varma said. The song went on air and be­came a hit, and Joel went on to make many more al­bums.
Varma told the story to show how much luck de­cides which art sur­vives. Bach, he noted, only be­came a big name decades after his death. {#bach}

quote.text: So there’s so much luck in­volved as well.

third.head: Blame the macroeconomists

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on why good times make bad music

body: Why is old music out­selling new? Ajay Shah has a half-joking the­ory: it is all the fault of the macroe­conomists.

They con­quered busi­ness cy­cles, he said, and Robert Lucas fa­mously de­clared after the re­sponse to the 2008 cri­sis that “we won”. {#lucas} “The Great Depression gave us Adolf Hitler. The 2008 cri­sis only gave us Donald Trump,” Shah said. {001-J10}
Music, he ar­gued, needed the angst and mis­ery of bad times as fuel, so great music would now come from Russia, China and the hor­ri­ble places of the world.

Amit Varma said they were for­tu­nate to have es­caped such times, though many peo­ple in India still live through them. Shah pointed to Rabindranath Tagore, per­son­ally priv­i­leged but wired into a dif­fi­cult time, and con­cluded that good art may be counter-cyclical. {001-C13}

quote.text: We are mas­ters of our own des­tiny be­cause to some ex­tent we’re able to in­ter­ro­gate and mod­ify that op­er­at­ing sys­tem.

box.title: The essay behind the uncles
box.text: Paul Graham’s *The Four Quadrants of Conformism*[[x6]][[x5]] sorts peo­ple into con­ven­tional-minded and in­de­pen­dent-minded, each pas­sive or ag­gres­sive. Amit Varma called it one of the finest es­says he has read in re­cent years, by “such a won­der­ful essay writer”. {001-R03}

sections.label: Nature and nurture
sections.head: Code we can rewrite
sections.caption: culture as a human operating system
body: Animals do bru­tal things, and no­body judges them for it. Seagulls, Ajay Shah said, kill pi­geons, and have been re­ported goug­ing out the eyes of seals. {001-S04}

Yet hu­mans are an­i­mals too, Amit Varma ob­served, and ev­ery­thing they do is morally judged. Much of what we call rea­son­ing is re­ally ra­tio­nal­i­sa­tion for wher­ever our in­stincts take us. He quoted Steven Pinker: “Nature gives us knobs, nur­ture turns them.” {001-J14}[[x8]][[x7]]
## Hardware and soft­ware

Shah saw a deeper dif­fer­ence. A new­born king cobra is a hun­dred per cent king cobra at birth: it can bite and kill, and its code stays the same for the rest of its life. Humans add an op­er­at­ing sys­tem of cul­ture, learned be­hav­iours, be­liefs and heuris­tics, and are unique in being able to in­ter­ro­gate and mod­ify it. {001-C01}

Varma took the metaphor as sup­port for his own point: char­ac­ter is con­tin­gent. Still, a so­ci­ety needs an eth­i­cal code that pun­ishes the bad and re­wards the good, he said, so we must be­have as if peo­ple are re­spon­si­ble even if, at the deep­est level, they are not. {001-C02}

~ Shah set­tled on shades of grey. We are each works in progress, he said; when an event am­bushes us we act on in­stinct, and growth lies in ask­ing af­ter­wards whether that in­stinct was right. {001-C03}

quote.text: We are mas­ters of our own des­tiny be­cause to some ex­tent we’re able to in­ter­ro­gate and mod­ify that op­er­at­ing sys­tem.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on culture as a human operating system

sections.label: Uncle watch
sections.head: The call of the uncle
sections.caption: uncles, anti-uncles and Galileo’s defiance
body: The writer Shrayana Bhattacharya once paid Amit Varma what he calls one of the finest com­pli­ments he has re­ceived: “Amit, you are an anti-uncle.” He lis­tens to the other side; an uncle is closed and in­sis­tent on his world­view. {001-S05}

Varma found the types mapped in Paul Graham’s essay[[x9]], which iden­ti­fies four kinds of mind by their calls, like species of birds. The ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded cry “Crush out­group!”; the pas­sively con­ven­tional ask what the neigh­bours will think; the pas­sively in­de­pen­dent say to each his own.

The ag­gres­sively in­de­pen­dent say *Eppur si muove*: still it turns. Galileo said it, Varma re­counted, after being forced to re­cant that the earth goes around the sun, look­ing up at the sky and stamp­ing the ground. {001-S06}
## Loud and un­o­rig­i­nal
The ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded, whether right-wingers or wokes, make the loud­est noise on so­cial media, Varma said, and stand in the way of progress. {001-C04}
His own provoca­tive col­umns had drawn them out, among them his ar­gu­ment that pop­u­la­tion is not India’s prob­lem, since peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs. {001-C05}

~ His rem­edy starts with him­self. His first re­sponse to a rad­i­cally new idea used to be no, he said, so he learned to fight that, be­cause every idea that changes the world is at first a rad­i­cal idea.

quote.text: The loud­est noise on Twitter and so­cial media is ac­tu­ally made by the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded. These are not peo­ple say­ing any­thing new.

art.caption: Amit Varma on uncles, anti-uncles and Galileo’s defiance

sections.label: Why uncles conform
sections.head: Not wood, not stones
sections.caption: uncles as optimisers, not true believers
body: Ajay Shah, a self-described card-carrying econ­o­mist, looks at un­cles as op­ti­mis­ers. People want the warmth of tribal net­works, he said, and loudly en­forc­ing so­cial norms is a ticket to power and suc­cess. {001-C07}

Many un­cles, in his view, are not deep be­liev­ers but are rid­ing an ide­ol­ogy, and will turn on a dime when the world changes. So he is kind to them. Amit Varma ac­cepted that as an ex­pla­na­tion, not a jus­ti­fi­ca­tion, since so­cial media am­pli­fies ev­ery­thing.
## Private truths

Shah drew on Timur Kuran’s pref­er­ence fal­si­fi­ca­tion[[x10]]. Three months be­fore com­mu­nism col­lapsed, ev­ery­one in East Germany and the USSR pro­fessed the of­fi­cial be­liefs, and no­body held them; some went along pas­sively, oth­ers ag­gres­sively po­liced vi­o­la­tors. {001-C08}

Varma reached for Kuran’s other phrase, the pref­er­ence cas­cade, to ex­plain the Modi wave. Indian so­ci­ety, he ar­gued, has al­ways been deeply il­lib­eral, and so­cial media showed closet big­ots that many oth­ers shared their views, so they no longer needed to hide them.
Shah, who stays away from so­cial media en­tirely, sep­a­rated two ques­tions: what should I do, and how is this phe­nom­e­non act­ing upon the world? {001-C10}
~ Criticism, Shah added, suf­fers from a mar­ket fail­ure: the critic pays a very high cost while cre­at­ing a pos­i­tive ex­ter­nal­ity for the world. {001-C09}

quote.text: But it was wise and ef­fi­cient to say that as a way to get along, as a way to gain power.

art.caption: Amit Varma on uncles as optimisers, not true believers

sections.label: The reading life
sections.head: One life is not enough
sections.caption: the extra lives that books give us
body: We make sense of the world by con­nect­ing dots[[x12]][[x11]], Amit Varma said. Personal ex­pe­ri­ence gives us very few, over many years; books give us many dots very fast, and fic­tion lets us live the lives of oth­ers.

His pick was Mark Haddon’s *The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time*, os­ten­si­bly a mur­der mys­tery told by a 15-year-old boy. Varma read out Haddon’s de­scrip­tion of it as “a novel about dif­fer­ence, about being an out­sider”. {001-R01}

Thomas Nagel’s essay *What Is It Like to Be a Bat?* ar­gued that we can de­scribe how a bat nav­i­gates by echolo­ca­tion but can never imag­ine it. {001-R05} With other peo­ple, Varma said, we do imag­ine, and mir­ror neu­rons wire us to em­pathise.
## An extra life

Ajay Shah ex­tended the ar­gu­ment be­yond fic­tion. The great non-fiction books are each the tra­jec­tory of one life, he said, so read­ing one is like liv­ing an extra life, the op­po­site of the prac­ti­tioner who lives the same day over and over.
~ Varma also re­jected the claim that peo­ple no longer read. There are mo­ments of short at­ten­tion spans, he said, but we all crave depth.

quote.text: I am made of all those books.

art.caption: Amit Varma on the extra lives that books give us

sections.label: Artists in amber
sections.head: Same song, older band
sections.caption: artists frozen in one old hit
body: Ajay Shah’s music pick was U2’s *Songs of Surrender*, 40 songs, mostly old, reimag­ined in a more grown-up way, with new ar­range­ments and edited lyrics. It is not a for­mula, he said, as *MTV Unplugged* is. {001-R02}
He liked the thought that some young lis­ten­ers might start here and only later go back to *The Joshua Tree*.

Amit Varma saw a larger point. Artists are forced to os­sify[[x13]] into one static ver­sion of them­selves. Radiohead, he said, are sick of per­form­ing *Creep*, writ­ten when they were im­ma­ture young men. {001-J21}

A big hit can be a curse, he said, echo­ing the mu­si­cian Gaurav Chintamani: you have changed, but “you’re os­si­fied into that one three-minute pack­age thing that you did twenty years ago.” {001-C12} Today bands can meet fans on Discord and change a song from day to day.
## No cross­ing twice
Shah ap­plied the idea to peo­ple: no man can cross the same river twice. {001-J19} When peo­ple are held to one crys­talline con­cep­tion of an idea, he said, it is not fair to their own jour­ney.
~ The Gandhi of 1919, he pointed out, was very dif­fer­ent from the Gandhi of 1939. {#gandhi}

quote.text: No man can cross the same river twice. He’s not the same and the river is not the same.

art.caption: Amit Varma on artists frozen in one old hit

quote.text: Because the critic per­son­ally takes the brunt of all the at­tacks that come by. But ac­tu­ally all the progress of the world is only made pos­si­ble by the crit­ics.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A snake’s tail, a thieving bird, a furious inbox and a lonely poet

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s run-in with village life
stories.head: Fear finds a fifth gear
body: Amit Varma, a city slicker by his own ac­count, has lately been liv­ing in a vil­lage, in a dis­trict he won’t name. The vil­lage bar­ber had al­ready taken the sides of his head. Then came the snake.

He was tak­ing rounds of Ajay Shah’s walk­ing track and had al­most run 7 km, walk­ing and run­ning by turns. He was com­pletely tired, and on the last stretch he thought he could not pos­si­bly go any faster. {#sevenk}
As he was cool­ing down, a snake whizzed out of the bushes on his right and into the bushes on his left. There it waited, its tail hang­ing out on the path.

Had it dis­ap­peared, Varma said, he would sim­ply have car­ried on. But the tail re­minded him of an Amitabh Bachchan and Shashi Kapoor film in which the two, bathing naked, are sur­prised by a woman at the door and cover the wrong part. “I thought this is a stupid snake, it thinks I can’t see it, but the tail is there.” {001-J02}
Then came a sec­ond thought: “play it safe, boy.” He turned around and sprinted madly. {001-S02}
His Garmin watch put the speed at about 25 kilo­me­tres an hour, which Shah later told him is the high­est speed man can at­tain.
~ Shah was un­moved. Varma, he said, would be a well-adjusted vil­lager when “the tail of a snake will no longer ex­cite peaks of phys­i­cal per­for­mance.” {001-J03}
stories.why: A tired body had more in re­serve than the tired mind be­lieved. The story also pre­views Shah’s point that when an event am­bushes us we act on in­stinct, and only af­ter­wards can ask whether the in­stinct was right. {001-C03}
stories.postscript: Varma in­sists he has no pre­ten­sions of being a well-adjusted vil­lager.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the snake’s tail

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s lakeside warning about a pretty bird
stories.head: Nice bird, nasty habits
body: By a lake­side in Udaipur, Ajay Shah once gave Amit Varma some shock­ing news about a bird Varma thought beau­ti­ful: “Seagulls are bas­tards.”

Seagulls look grace­ful, Shah ex­plained, and we ex­pect some nice veg­e­tar­ian bird. {001-S04} In fact they kill and eat pi­geons, gouge chunks of meat from the backs of baby whales, and have been re­ported goug­ing out the eyes of seals.

Varma added that seag­ulls go for the eyes first, and are lazy too: they steal food from oth­ers, which is “like steal­ing from a thief”. {001-J04} He thought of the License Raj state tax­ing its own rent-seekers.
~ Shah blamed our “an­thro­pocen­tric fail­ure”: what we ex­pect of a seag­ull and what it does are far apart, and the gap cre­ates cog­ni­tive dis­so­nance.
stories.why: We judge an­i­mals by how they look, and are un­set­tled when be­hav­iour and image part ways. From there, the hosts turned to why we don’t judge an­i­mals morally but do judge hu­mans. {001-C01}

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the price of a provocative column
stories.head: Thirty-five years, one insult
body: Amit Varma once wrote a col­umn ar­gu­ing, a bit provoca­tively, that it is im­moral to have chil­dren[[x14]]. People he had not heard from since school, 35 years ear­lier, found him on Facebook to tell him he was an ass­hole. {001-S07}

The ar­gu­ment rests on three things we would all ac­cept, he said: do noth­ing to any­one with­out con­sent, cause no one pain, and kill no one. A child is born with­out con­sent, will feel pain and will die. {001-R10}
So hav­ing chil­dren is prima facie im­moral, he ar­gued, and the ar­gu­ment must be tack­led, though he might well do things he thinks im­moral. “We are hu­mans, we are fucked up, that’s how it is.”
~ It was one of three col­umns that, Varma said, drew fu­ri­ous re­sponses from the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded.
stories.why: Arguing against re­ceived wis­dom in pub­lic has a per­sonal price. Ajay Shah’s point about crit­i­cism fol­lows: the critic takes the brunt of the at­tacks, while the progress the critic makes pos­si­ble be­longs to ev­ery­one. {001-C09}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the column that riled his old schoolmates

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the loneliness of being mobbed online
stories.head: Alone among a thousand
body: The poet Hussain Haidry, a guest on *The Seen and the Unseen*, was once mobbed on­line by right-wing ac­counts. He felt so alone, he told Amit Varma. {001-S08}
No one called to say they were with him, or to ask how he was feel­ing.

Varma has been the tar­get of right-wing mobs and woke mobs at dif­fer­ent times, and he knows the feel­ing. He has many well-wishers, he said, but no one re­alises what you are going through when, within an hour, a thou­sand peo­ple are abus­ing you and retweet­ing you. {#mob}
~ Such mob be­hav­iour, he ar­gued, has a chill­ing ef­fect on dis­course: peo­ple stop say­ing the things they feel, until ul­ti­mately they don’t even feel that way any­more. {#chill}
stories.why: Mobs iso­late their tar­gets. Even a writer with many well-wishers can feel alone when the abuse ar­rives all at once, and that kind of mob be­hav­iour, Varma ar­gued, chills what ev­ery­one else is will­ing to say.
stories.postscript: Varma’s full con­ver­sa­tion with Haidry is Episode 275 of *The Seen and the Unseen*, ti­tled *Hindustani Musalmaan*.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Hussain Haidry’s loneliness

quiz.q: Which of India’s big four venomous snakes strikes with no reasonable provocation, says Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: The Russell’s viper; the cobra and krait, he said, are quite mild.

quiz.q: How fast did Amit Varma’s Garmin watch say he sprinted after spotting the snake’s tail?
quiz.a: About 25 kilo­me­tres an hour, which Shah told him is the high­est speed man can at­tain.

quiz.q: What compliment did Shrayana Bhattacharya pay Amit Varma at a book event?
quiz.a: She called him an anti-uncle: open-minded, will­ing to change and to en­gage any­one.

quiz.q: In Paul Graham’s essay, what is the call of the aggressively conventional-minded?
quiz.a: “Crush out­group!”, alarm­ing, Graham notes, for its ex­cla­ma­tion point after a vari­able.

quiz.q: Which scholar coined “preference falsification”, the idea Ajay Shah used to explain the Soviet collapse?
quiz.a: Timur Kuran, de­scrib­ing be­liefs pro­fessed in pub­lic but held by no­body in pri­vate.

quiz.q: Which band, according to Amit Varma, is sick of performing its early hit “Creep”?
quiz.a: Radiohead, who wrote it when they were “im­ma­ture young men”, Varma said.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 1. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Galileo Galilei (Justus Sustermans, public domain); Paul Graham (Sarah Harlin, public domain); Billy Joel (David Shankbone, CC BY 3.0); Mark Haddon (PhilipRomano, CC BY-SA 4.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Apple and Spotify.

shelf.title: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time
shelf.creator: Mark Haddon
shelf.why: It shows what fic­tion can do: let you live in­side a very dif­fer­ent mind.

shelf.title: Songs of Surrender
shelf.creator: U2
shelf.why: U2 re­think songs they wrote as kids from a more grown-up place, chang­ing ar­range­ments and lyrics in­stead of stay­ing frozen in the fa­mous ver­sions.

shelf.title: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Paul Graham’s two-axis map of thinkers (con­ven­tional or in­de­pen­dent, pas­sive or ag­gres­sive) that sin­gles out the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded as the loud­est voices and the real ob­sta­cle to new ideas.

shelf.title: Private Truths, Public Lies
shelf.creator: Timur Kuran
shelf.why: Kuran’s the­ory of pref­er­ence fal­si­fi­ca­tion and pref­er­ence cas­cades: regimes look unan­i­mously sup­ported until peo­ple dis­cover that oth­ers se­cretly dis­agree too.

shelf.title: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
shelf.creator: Thomas Nagel
shelf.why: Nagel’s essay ar­gu­ing that we can un­der­stand in­tel­lec­tu­ally how a bat nav­i­gates by echolo­ca­tion but can never imag­ine being one.

shelf.title: The Tell-Tale Brain
shelf.creator: VS Ramachandran
shelf.why: It ex­plains the sci­ence be­hind em­pa­thy: mir­ror neu­rons copy the ex­pe­ri­ences of oth­ers when we hear about them.

shelf.title: Lessons from an Ankhon Dekhi Prime Minister
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s case for read­ing: ex­pe­ri­ence gives us only a few dots, slowly, while books let us col­lect many dots fast, live many lives and reach deep, com­plex truths about the world that ex­pe­ri­ence alone can’t.

shelf.title: Population Is Not a Problem, but Our Greatest Strength
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s chal­lenge to the school les­son that pop­u­la­tion is India’s big­gest prob­lem: peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs, pop­u­la­tion den­sity drives pros­per­ity, and the ills blamed on pop­u­la­tion are fail­ures of gov­er­nance.

shelf.title: India’s Problem Is Poverty, Not Inequality
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit sep­a­rates two prob­lems peo­ple rou­tinely con­fuse and that need op­po­site so­lu­tions: in a pos­i­tive-sum world in­equal­ity can rise while poverty falls, as in India after 1991, so end­ing poverty through growth is the real moral im­per­a­tive.

shelf.title: It Is Immoral to Have Children. Here’s Why
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s de­lib­er­ately provoca­tive col­umn: we agree not to act on peo­ple with­out con­sent, cause pain or kill, yet a child is born with­out con­sent and will suf­fer and die.

shelf.title: Kashi Ka Assi
shelf.creator: Kashinath Singh
shelf.why: A line from Kashinath Singh’s book, about play­ing your har­mo­nium while the world goes to hell, gives Amit his stance on so­cial media: block the toxic ac­counts and build a feed of the finest minds.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Desperately Seeking Shah Rukh
shelf.creator: Shrayana Bhattacharya
shelf.why: Shrayana Bhattacharya uses Indian women’s ado­ra­tion of Shah Rukh Khan as a lens on Indian so­ci­ety and how lonely its women are; Amit says it ‘con­tains multitudes’, from eco­nom­ics and so­ci­ol­ogy to beau­ti­ful writ­ing.

shelf.title: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shrayana Bhattacharya
shelf.why: Amit’s most pop­u­lar Seen and the Unseen episode, a con­ver­sa­tion with Shrayana Bhattacharya (who gave him the ‘anti-uncle’ label) on the eco­nomic and so­cial lives of Indian women.

shelf.title: Hussain Haidry, Hindustani Musalmaan (Episode 275 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Hussain Haidry
shelf.why: It is a fuller con­ver­sa­tion with the poet whose ex­pe­ri­ence shows what on­line mobs do to the peo­ple they tar­get.

shelf.title: In a Silent Way (Episode 316 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Gaurav Chintamani
shelf.why: Musician Gaurav Chintamani on how a big hit can be­come a curse (you keep chang­ing, but au­di­ences keep shout­ing for a three-minute song from twenty years ago) and on whether orig­i­nal­ity even ex­ists.

shelf.title: Eric Weinstein Won’t Toe the Line (Episode 330 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Eric Weinstein
shelf.why: It is the longer ver­sion of the de­bate this episode ends on: with far more po­ten­tial artists alive than ever be­fore, why don’t we see more great art?

shelf.title: Is Old Music Killing New Music?
shelf.creator: Ted Gioia
shelf.why: Gioia’s data shows old music is out­selling new music by a mile.

shelf.title: The Time a Stiff Caught Fire
shelf.creator: Keith Yates
shelf.why: It tells the full story of the fan who got ‘Piano Man’ onto the radio and saved Billy Joel’s ca­reer, which shows how much luck de­cides what we later call great art.

shelf.title: Beat a Drum
shelf.creator: R.E.M.
shelf.why: It is the source of the episode’s cen­tral image of peo­ple as un­fin­ished works in progress.

shelf.title: YouTube Music (discovery playlists)
shelf.why: You just ask it for a playlist with­out hav­ing to think, and it brings you new things.

shelf.title: The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s long-form pod­cast of three-to-eight-hour deep dives, con­ver­sa­tions no gate­keeper would have com­mis­sioned, which have be­come an oral his­tory of India; its show notes list every book men­tioned.

laughs.text: Amit says he wants the show to cover ‘not just about the pro­found, but also the profane’. Ajay’s im­me­di­ate reply: ‘How did you get that in­ter­est­ing hair­cut?’

Amit com­pares the snake with its tail stick­ing out to a scene in an Amitabh Bachchan–Shashi Kapoor film where the two are bathing naked, a woman opens the door, and they cover the wrong thing: ‘this is a stupid snake, it thinks I can’t see it, but the tail is there.’
Ajay on Amit’s 25 km/h sprint: he’ll be a well-adjusted vil­lager when ‘the tail of a snake will no longer ex­cite peaks of phys­i­cal per­for­mance.’

Amit says seag­ulls are not just bas­tards but ‘lazy bastards’, be­cause they steal food from oth­ers, ‘like steal­ing from a thief’. He com­pares this to the License Raj state tax­ing the rent-seekers and cronies it had cre­ated.
Amit on who gets to be an ‘uncle’: only men can be un­cles, while ‘women can be Karens, I guess.’
Paul Graham’s line, read by Amit, on the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded whose call is ‘Crush out­group!’: ‘It’s rather alarm­ing to see an ex­cla­ma­tion point after a vari­able.’
Ajay on how far macro­eco­nomics has come: ‘The Great Depression gave us Adolf Hitler. The 2008 cri­sis only gave us Donald Trump. Okay, so we’ve clearly come a long way.’
‘Halfway from coal, half­way to diamond’, Ajay’s image of peo­ple as works in progress and the episode’s title, is taken from the R.E.M. song ‘Beat a Drum’.
Steven Pinker, quoted by Amit: ‘Nature gives us knobs, nur­ture turns them.’
Galileo’s ‘Eppur si muove’ (‘and still it turns’), which Paul Graham uses as the call of the ag­gres­sively in­de­pen­dent-minded.

Glenn Reynolds, the blog­ger known as Instapundit, whom Amit cites as ar­gu­ing that Trump’s rise came from let­ting xeno­pho­bia into the open. If Trump could say Mexicans are rapists, peo­ple with sim­i­lar prej­u­dices could em­brace him.
Robert Lucas, cited by Ajay, say­ing ‘we won’ about the re­sponse to the 2008 cri­sis, as ev­i­dence that macroe­conomists have tamed the busi­ness cycle.
‘No man can cross the same river twice. He’s not the same and the river is not the same.’ Ajay uses it to argue that ideas and peo­ple should not be frozen at one mo­ment.
Radiohead being sick of per­form­ing ‘Creep’, a break­away hit writ­ten when they were ‘im­ma­ture young men’, which Amit cites as an artist trapped by an old song.
